Enthalpy.  Physical chemistry, which I taught, is really made up of three main areas: thermodynamics, quantum mechanics, and statistical mechanics, which ties thermo and quantum together.

Enthalpy is one of six fundamental measures of a system:  Enthalpy, Entropy, Gibbs (free) energy, Helmholtz (work) energy, Temperature and Pressure.  

The reason Enthalpy is important for chemistry is because in a chemical reaction done under conditions of constant pressure and temperature (the most common case), the heat released or absorbed during the reaction is the change in Enthalpy.

Some chemical changes produce heat, like burning methane or hydrogen in the presence of oxygen.  These changes are called exothermic.  A few changes absorb heat.  These are called endothermic, and the reaction uses heat from the surroundings.  The heat absorbed or released in these reactions is the enthalpy change.

An example of a heat-consuming chemical change is the phase change from liquid water to water vapor.  That consumes a large amount of heat, and is why we perspire.  The water evaporating from our skin uses our body heat to turn liquid water to water vapor, thereby cools us off.

It's also why steam is so dangerous.  When water vapor condenses on a surface like our skin, it releases that heat, causing burns even more severe than it would otherwise.

OK. I've thought about this overnight, and I think I have an insight on why this puzzle stirred up so much controversy here in the comments. 

Basically, it boils down to it being _too_ themed! 

A themed Sunday puzzle generally has (per A.I. answer from Google) "6 to 8+ longer theme answers". This puzzle had fourteen - significantly higher than average!

On top of that, multiple of them depend on visual design elements in the grid that only help if you're familiar with how to play the game. Three of those reference the question mark boxes in a way that makes them only solvable from crosses for non-players, and another 2 were paired clues where the only apparent connection was a pair of green shapes that could be lots of things (bolts? tubes? weird capital letter 'T's? ...  who can tell?). Only after you solve 14D (from the crosses, of course) does it become clear that those are both pipes, and a travel mechanism.

And then there's the brick design of most of the "black" squares. We non-gamers can surmise that the design must be related to the theme, but that adds nothing to the solving experience, so just feels like a distracting annoyance.

So I don't think it was so much the subject of the theme. I don't even think think it was the 'old vs young' dichotomy that's been tossed about. I think it was that the relentless ubiquity of the theme elements aimed _only_ at those who are very familiar with a particular game, felt like an in-joke designed to exclude everyone else.

All I have to say is, Really?  I have read the NYT for 40 yrs, and played the crossword since retirement.  I have never played video games because I was too busy earning a living.   I know the NYT is trying to attract younger readers, and I have sympathy for that.  But PLEASE wait for we baby boomers to die before you give us another puzzle like this.

Oh man, if I'd had you guys as students--I might still be teaching.  You caught me in a weasel.  What do I mean by "it would otherwise"?  Wonderful question.

Elements form "families" with similar behavior.  The oxygen (O) family has O, S (sulfur), Se (selenium), and Te (tellurium).  I'm going to ignore Po (polonium), not because it doesn't fit, but because it's so rare.

All these form hydrides of the form H2X, where X = O, S, Se, or Te.  

Generally speaking, the inter-molecular forces increase with number of electrons, or, similarly, in how heavy they are. So we'd expect the intermolecular forces to be greatest in H2Te, and weakest in H2O.

The strength of the inter-molecular forces is seen in the boiling point, where we take molecules in close association and separate them.

H2Te has a boiling point of -2.2 C (Celcius).  It's a gas at room temperature.  H2Se has a boiling point of -41 C.  Lower, as we'd expect, because H2Se is considerably lighter than H2Te.  

H2S, hydrogen sulfide, lighter yet, has a boiling point of -60C, so even lower than H2Se.

We'd *expect* based on these trends, that water, H2O, would have a boiling less than -60C, but in fact it comes out a whooping 160 Celcius degrees *higher* than the trend line would indicate.

So water has as extremely anomalous boiling point.  That's what I mean "it would otherwise".

By the way, the same thing happens in the nitrogen family.  NH3 has a much higher boiling point than PH3 (phosphine).

@Tom R The question mark blocks in Mario games are a source of resources for the titular character. Question mark blocks appear in a row of bricks, like how they're depicted in this grid. When the character jumps up and hits a block, something useful for the player comes out of the top of the block. These could include coins (which increase the player's score), one-ups (which grant the player another opportunity to try to win if they fail), or occasionally, even a vine (which grows directly up and out of the block, offering the player a new route to explore by climbing up the vine like a ladder).

In short, the question mark blocks aren't stand-ins here. Each answer above a question mark block is a resource that emerges vertically from said block in the video game, which makes it a pretty clever visual nod for fans of the series.
